According to arXiv 2603.26983, a technical challenge that arises when applying Art. 50 II watermarking to synthetic data used for AI training is the fundamental tension between human-readable labeling and machine-readability. Watermarks designed to be discernible to humans can impede the training of AI models, as they may evolve into features that the AI systems learn to recognize, jeopardizing the integrity of the training data. This creates a conflict between the regulatory requirement for persistent labeling and the technical need for clean, unadulterated data in model training pipelines.

In comparison, fact-checking systems face a different marking challenge. The iterative nature of editorial workflows in fact-checking leads to the degradation of marking signals, as human editorial intervention destroys the provenance chains that machine-readable marking requires. Unlike the synthetic data case, where a dual-version solution can separate marked and unmarked outputs, no equivalent architectural solution exists for fact-checking pipelines, making it difficult to maintain clear distinctions between AI-generated and human-authored content. 

Thus, while both cases highlight the difficulties of maintaining effective marking under regulatory requirements, the specific challenges differ: synthetic data generation struggles with the integrity of training data due to watermarking, whereas fact-checking systems struggle with the loss of marking integrity due to human editorial processes.
